title: Guardrails & Production Safety
summary: Keeping an LLM feature safe and auditable once real users can type anything into it.

slides.markdown:
Once real users can type anything into a prompt, "the model is well-behaved in my tests" stops being enough — production LLM features need **guardrails** on both ends of the pipeline, human oversight for high-stakes actions, and a record of what happened and why.

- **Input guardrails** — catch malicious or manipulative user input before it reaches the model.
- **Output guardrails** — catch unsafe or malformed model output before it reaches the user or a downstream system.
- **Logging** — the only way to reconstruct "why did it do that" after the fact.

slides.subTitle: Detecting prompt injection and jailbreaks
slides.markdown:
**Input guardrails** screen what reaches the model: a **classifier** (rule-based or a smaller model) checks incoming text for known jailbreak patterns ("ignore previous instructions," role-play framings designed to bypass safety behavior) and prompt-injection attempts hidden in pasted content, flagging or blocking suspicious input before it's ever added to the prompt.

This is inherently an arms race — new jailbreak phrasing appears faster than any static rule list can be maintained — so input guardrails are a meaningful first layer, not a complete solution on their own.

slides.subTitle: Content filtering, PII redaction, schema validation
slides.markdown:
**Output guardrails** check what the model produced before it reaches the user or a downstream action: content filters catch unsafe or off-brand text, PII detectors redact accidentally-leaked sensitive data (a phone number from retrieved context, a customer's email in an unrelated answer), and schema validators reject a structured response that doesn't match the expected format before it hits application code.

Output guardrails are the last line of defense — even well-guarded input can still produce a bad output for reasons unrelated to injection, like a plain factual or formatting mistake.

slides.subTitle: Human-in-the-loop for high-stakes actions
slides.markdown:
For actions that are **irreversible, financial, or high-stakes** (sending an email on the user's behalf, issuing a refund, deleting data), the safest architecture inserts a mandatory human confirmation step between the model's proposed action and its execution — the model drafts the action, a human approves or rejects it.

This isn't a lack of trust in the model specifically; it's a recognition that any automated system, LLM or not, should have a human checkpoint before an action that can't be cheaply undone. Save full autonomy for actions that are cheap to reverse.

slides.subTitle: Rate limiting for AI APIs
slides.markdown:
AI features add a dimension to standard rate limiting: each request has a real, sometimes substantial per-call cost, so unlimited access is both an abuse vector (scripted thousands of calls) and a direct cost problem, not just load management. Limits typically apply per user, per API key, and sometimes per estimated token cost, not just raw request count.

This connects to general resilience patterns (throttling, backoff, circuit breakers) — AI endpoints just make skipping rate limits far costlier per abused request than a typical API call.

slides.subTitle: Logging and reconstructing "why did it do that"
slides.markdown:
When an agent or LLM feature does something wrong in production, you need to reconstruct exactly what happened: the full prompt sent (including any retrieved context), every tool call and its arguments, every observation returned, and the final output — logged with enough fidelity to replay the reasoning after the fact.

Without this, debugging a bad production incident becomes guesswork; with it, you can pinpoint exactly which retrieved chunk, tool result, or reasoning step led the model astray, and add that case to your eval set so it's caught automatically next time.

slides.subTitle: The system prompt alone is not a security boundary
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Telling the model in the system prompt to never reveal secrets or break character is sufficient protection."

**Why it's wrong:** the model weighs the system prompt probabilistically alongside user input, not as an enforced rule — a crafted message (role-play framing, a claimed "debug mode") can still push past it. Prompt wording alone treats a soft suggestion as a security control.

**Correct model:** treat the system prompt as one weak layer — pair it with input/output guardrails, least-privilege access, and jailbreak monitoring.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: where each guardrail layer catches failures
slides.markdown:
| Layer | Catches | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| Input guardrail | Known jailbreak phrasing, obvious injection attempts | Novel phrasing, injection hidden in retrieved documents |
| Output guardrail | Unsafe content, leaked PII, malformed structure | Subtly wrong but well-formatted answers |
| Human-in-the-loop | Any single high-stakes action before it executes | Doesn't scale to every low-stakes interaction |
| Rate limiting | Scripted abuse, runaway cost | A single well-crafted malicious request |

**How to decide:** no single layer is sufficient on its own — each one covers a gap the others leave open, which is exactly why production systems stack all four rather than picking one.

slides.subTitle: Actively trying to break your own system
slides.markdown:
**Red-teaming** means deliberately attacking your own feature before real users (or real attackers) do: writing adversarial prompts designed to leak the system prompt, extract another user's data, or trigger a disallowed action, then feeding every success back into the guardrails and the eval set.

A useful discipline is treating each successful jailbreak as a bug report, not a one-off curiosity — add it to the golden test set from [Evaluating LLM Systems](evaluating-llm-systems) so a regression in that exact attack is caught automatically on every future change, instead of relying on someone remembering to retest it by hand.
